hero.title: File:Marine deities Gandhara 1st century.jpg
hero.credit: Own work, photographed at the MET
hero.description: Marine_deities or Boatmen. Pakistan (probably Swat Valley) ca.1st_century. Serpentinite, H. 6 5/8 in. (16.8 cm); W. 17 in. (43.2 cm). This sculpture embellished the stairways of a stupa, likely on the western end of the Swat Valley. The treatment of the anatomy is interesting in terms of naturalism and schematization of the musculature. (notice du musée en 2015)

gallery.title: File:Standing Bodhisattva Gandhara Musee Guimet.jpg
gallery.credit: Own work Personal photograph, 2004, background retouched.
gallery.description: Standing Bodhisattva (Fr. Bodhisattva Debout). Pakistan, Gandharan art, site of Shahbaz-Garhi. The identity of the bodhisattva is not known, so the work is is simply titled "Standing Bodhisattva." The representation is of a standard bodhisattva of the Gandharan style, displaying the fearlessness mudra. No clear indicator identifies the figure as one bodhisattva or another. The Musée Guimet suggests that it may be Gautama or Avalokiteshvara.

gallery.filename: Dīpaṁkara Jātaka. Bezeklik Cave 9, Furfan, China. Ninth-eleventh centuries. Wall painting.png
gallery.title: File:Dīpaṁkara Jātaka. Bezeklik Cave 9, Furfan, China. Ninth-eleventh centuries. Wall painting.png
gallery.description:
The Dīpaṁkara Jātaka is one of the best-known jātakas of the Buddha. In a remote past eon Śākyamuni was born as a Brahman youth called Megha. The king at that time monopolized the flower market in order to offer all flowers to Buddha Dīpaṁkara himself. Yet Megha managed to find some flowers and offered them to Dīpaṁkara. In addition, when Dīpaṁkara was about to pass a muddy road, Megha unfurled his hair onto the mud for the Buddha to step on. Having received these offerings from Megha, Dīpaṁkara predicted for the young Brahmin a future Buddhahood. ... In this painting from Bezeklik (Figure 9), on the right side of Dīpaṁkara Buddha, Megha is shown standing holding flowers in his hands and he is shown again kneeling down laying his hair under the feet of Dīpaṁkara. The most recognizable exclusive attribute of this painting for identification is the hair.
(Zhu, Tianshu (12 July 2012), "Reshaping the Jātaka Stories: From Jātakas to Avadānas and Praṇidhānas in Paintings at Kucha and Turfan", Buddhist Studies Review, 29 (1): 73, doi:10.1558/bsrv.v29i1.57)
